heroText: Montevideo is Uruguay's calm coastal capital, built around the Rambla, old port streets, football culture and relaxed neighborhoods facing the Rio de la Plata. Start in Ciudad Vieja, eat at Mercado del Puerto, then follow the Rambla of Montevideo toward Pocitos Beach. Carrasco airport is straightforward, and the city works well before or after Colonia and Punta del Este.

areas.name: Ciudad Vieja
areas.text: Ciudad Vieja is best for history, port restaurants, museums and daytime walking, though nights are quieter outside key streets.

areas.name: Centro
areas.text: Centro is practical for Avenida 18 de Julio, theatres, transport and better value than the waterfront neighborhoods.

areas.name: Pocitos
areas.text: Pocitos is the easiest first base for beach walks, restaurants, safer evenings and modern apartment-style stays.

areas.name: Punta Carretas
areas.text: Punta Carretas is upscale and walkable, with malls, dining, Rambla access and a quieter feel than Centro.

areas.name: Carrasco
areas.text: Carrasco is elegant and residential, close to the airport and beach but farther from old-city sights.

airports.name: Carrasco International Airport (MVD)
airports.text: Carrasco airport is east of central Montevideo; transfers are usually manageable, especially for Carrasco, Pocitos and Punta Carretas stays.

airportTransfer.value: 30-45 min by taxi, airport shuttle or ride-hail to central Montevideo
airportTransfer.distance: about 20 km east of the city centre

stayOverview: Pocitos is the easiest first Montevideo base for beach walks, restaurants and safer evenings, while Punta Carretas is polished and walkable. Ciudad Vieja and Centro suit history and value, and Carrasco works for quiet airport-side stays.
hotelIntro: Montevideo hotel choice is pleasantly simple: use Pocitos or Punta Carretas for most leisure stays, Ciudad Vieja for history, Centro for value and theatres, or Carrasco when airport access and quiet beach streets matter.
rentalCars: A rental car is unnecessary inside Montevideo, but useful for Punta del Este, wineries or coastal road trips.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Pocitos or Punta Carretas for a first stay because the Rambla, restaurants and evening walks are easy.

travelTips.title: Rambla time
travelTips.text: Keep the Montevideo plan compact: group nearby sights together and leave enough time for transfers, meals and weather changes.

travelTips.title: Weekend pace
travelTips.text: Ciudad Vieja can be quiet on weekends and evenings, so check restaurant hours before planning dinner there.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Colonia is easy by bus or car, while Punta del Este needs a longer beach-focused day or overnight.

history.text: Between 1680 and 1683, Portugal founded the city of Colonia do Sacramento in the region across the bay from Buenos Aires.

history.label: 18th century
history.text: Until the end of the 18th century, Montevideo remained a fortified area, today known as Ciudad Vieja. 19th century On 3 February 1807, British troops under the command of General Samuel Auchmuty and Admiral.
On 22 November 1723, Field Marshal Manuel de Freitas da Fonseca of Portugal built the Montevieu fort.

On 22 January 1724, the Spanish forced the Portuguese to abandon the location and started populating the city, initially with six families moving in from Buenos Aires and soon thereafter by families arriving from.
During the May Revolution of 1810 and the subsequent uprising of the provinces of Rio de la Plata, the Spanish colonial government moved to Montevideo.
In 1816, Portugal invaded the recently liberated territory and in 1821, it was annexed to the Banda Oriental of Brazil.
Juan Antonio Lavalleja and his band called the Treinta y Tres Orientales ("Thirty-Three Orientals") re-established the independence of the region in 1825.
Uruguay was consolidated as an independent state in 1828, with Montevideo as the nation's capital.
In 1829, the demolition of the city's fortifications began and plans were made for an extension beyond the Ciudad Vieja, referred to as the "Ciudad Nueva" ("new city").
When the Portuguese invaded the Banda Oriental and annexed it as the province of Cisplatina until 1831, they called the city Montevidéu, and pronounced as .
In 1838, Oribe was forced to resign from the presidency; he established a rebel army and began a long civil war, the Guerra Grande, which lasted until 1851.
In 1853 a stagecoach bus line was established joining Montevideo with the newly formed settlement of Unión and the first natural gas street lights were inaugurated.
